My own independent result (computed from the task numbers 4, 7, 9 with python3 via Bash, result [S2]). No verdict is given here.

Independent recomputation table (M1 = Machine 1, M2 = Machine 2; each job runs on exactly one machine per row):
| # | M1 jobs | M2 jobs | Load M1 | Load M2 | Makespan | Sum |
|1| 4,7,9 | none | 20 | 0 | 20 | 20 |
|2| 4,7 | 9 | 11 | 9 | 11 | 20 |
|3| 4,9 | 7 | 13 | 7 | 13 | 20 |
|4| 4 | 7,9 | 4 | 16 | 16 | 20 |
|5| 7,9 | 4 | 16 | 4 | 16 | 20 |
|6| 7 | 4,9 | 7 | 13 | 13 | 20 |
|7| 9 | 4,7 | 9 | 11 | 11 | 20 |
|8| none | 4,7,9 | 0 | 20 | 20 | 20 |

Key facts (all derived from [S2] output):
- There are 8 rows (2^3). Each job appears exactly once per row, and every row's loads sum to 4+7+9 = 20.
- The minimum makespan is 11. It occurs in rows 2 and 7 only.
- The optimal assignment is {4,7} on one machine (load 11) and {9} on the other (load 9). Row 2 puts {4,7} on M1 and row 7 puts it on M2. These two rows are the same up to swapping the machines.
- Symmetry: swapping the machine labels maps row i to row 9−i. The 8 rows therefore form 4 mirror pairs: (1,8), (2,7), (3,6), (4,5). The 4 distinct partitions have makespans 20, 11, 13 and 16.
- Lower bound: the total is 20, so the makespan is at least 20/2 = 10. A makespan of 10 would need a subset summing to exactly 10. The subset sums are 0, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13, 16, 20 [S2], and none of them is 10. The largest of the two loads must therefore be at least 11, because loads are integers and the nearest subset sums to 10 are 9 (the other machine would then carry 11) and 11. So 11 is optimal.
- Also, the makespan is at least the longest job, which is 9, and that bound is weaker.
